comments.author: ssal_pt
comments.body_html:
I found the mod description very interesting. I use ammo added by mods, and I have a question.

Ammo added by mods is usually a clone of the base vanilla ammo. Does mod ammo follow the fragmentation pattern of the base vanilla ammo?

For example, let’s look at the Ammo_config.json for WTT - Content Backport. The 7.62x25mm TT M995 (68c15f77ed3d7df9220debd6) ammo is an itemTplToClone of the 7.62x25mm TT AKBS (5735fdcd2459776445391d61). Therefore, I am wondering if, when the Content Backport 7.62x25mm TT M995 hits something and fragments, it follows the fragmentation pattern of the vanilla 7.62x25mm TT AKBS.

comments.author: EchoStarz
comments.body_html:
The short answer is no, cloned ammo from other mods does not inherit RealisticFrag’s behavior. The longer “why” matters, since it’s two separate questions in one:

Does RealisticFrag override the cloned ammo? RealisticFrag works by exact template-ID lookup. The 7.62×25 AKBS entry (5735fdcd2459776445391d61) is in my config, so AKBS gets the modified frag chance and velocity gating. The WTT-Content-Backport M995 has its own unique template ID (68c15f77ed3d7df9220debd6), and that ID is not in my config, so neither the server-side override nor the client-side velocity gate runs for it. The same applies to any modded ammo cloned from a vanilla parent.

Does the clone at least inherit the modified base values? Also no. When SPT clones an item via itemTplToClone, it deep-copies the source’s _props at the moment the clone runs and registers the result as a fully independent template. RealisticFrag declares [Injectable(TypePriority = OnLoadOrder.PostDBModLoader + 1)], which makes it run one tick after the standard PostDBModLoader priority that cloning mods use, so cloning happens first against vanilla AKBS. Realisticfrag modifies the AKBS template afterward, and the clone keeps its original snapshot. Even if the order were reversed, the clone would only carry a frozen snapshot of whatever values existed at clone time; it wouldn’t track later edits to the parent.

comments.author: EchoStarz
comments.body_html: Mechanically, when a bullet “fragments” in EFT, it stops behaving like a single projectile that deals damage to one body part and instead breaks apart inside the target. The engine spawns several extra damage events across the body zones surrounding the hit, using the round’s MinFragmentsCount and MaxFragmentsCount values to decide how many fragments. So a single torso shot from a fragmenting round can deal damage to the thorax, stomach, and an arm in one hit, rather than just punching a clean hole through the thorax. The wound channel is wider, more body parts get hit, and bleeding is more likely to land on multiple zones
